2025.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Motegi, 28 September 2025, five rounds to spare
2025.note: Marc Márquez ended the longest wait of his career at Motegi on 28 September 2025, taking second behind Ducati teammate Francesco Bagnaia to settle the title with five rounds still to run. It was his seventh premier-class crown, drawing him level with Valentino Rossi, and his first since 2019: a gap of 2,184 days that contained four operations. Eleven grand prix wins and fourteen sprint victories made him Ducati's fourth MotoGP champion, and the rider he beat to it was his brother Álex.

2024.clinched: Solidarity Grand Prix, Barcelona, 17 November 2024, final round
2024.note: The 2024 title went to the last race of the year, moved from flood-hit Valencia to Barcelona, where Jorge Martín needed only a top-nine finish and took third. Bagnaia won the race, his eleventh victory of the season, and still lost the championship by ten points, because Martín had spent the year collecting podiums rather than wins: sixteen in grands prix against three victories. He became the first rider of the MotoGP era to take the title on a satellite bike.

2023.clinched: Valencian Community Grand Prix, Valencia, 26 November 2023, final round
2023.note: Bagnaia reached the Valencia finale twenty-one points clear and left it champion in abrupt fashion. Jorge Martín, who had won Saturday's sprint to cut the gap to fourteen, crashed into Marc Márquez while fighting for fifth on lap six. Bagnaia won the race, his seventh of the year, to become the first Ducati rider with two MotoGP titles and the first back-to-back champion since Márquez in 2019.

2022.clinched: Valencian Community Grand Prix, Valencia, 6 November 2022, final round
2022.note: Bagnaia's first title was a salvage job. Four retirements in the first ten rounds left him ninety-one points behind Fabio Quartararo after the German Grand Prix, the largest deficit any champion has overturned since the current points system arrived in 1993. Four straight wins from Assen onwards flipped it, and at Valencia he needed only to finish fourteenth. Ninth place did it. He called it the hardest race of his life, and it was Ducati's first riders' title since 2007.

2021.clinched: Emilia Romagna Grand Prix, Misano, 24 October 2021, two rounds to spare
2021.note: Quartararo became the first French rider to win the premier class at Misano on 24 October 2021, and did it from fifteenth on the grid. He carved through to fourth while his only remaining rival, Bagnaia, crashed out of the lead with five laps left at the corner that had already caught his teammate. At twenty-two, Quartararo ended a run of nine consecutive Spanish champions and gave Yamaha its first title since 2015.

2020.clinched: Valencian Community Grand Prix, Valencia, 15 November 2020, one round to spare
2020.note: The strangest season of the modern era produced its most consistent champion. Joan Mir won a single race all year, the European Grand Prix, fewer than any premier-class champion before him, and sealed the title with seventh place at Valencia on 15 November 2020 with a round still to run. Nine different riders won races across thirteen rounds, Márquez was absent from the second round onwards with a broken arm, and Suzuki had its first champion since Kenny Roberts Jr in 2000.

2019.clinched: Thailand Grand Prix, Buriram, 6 October 2019, four rounds to spare
2019.note: Márquez settled 2019 by beating rookie Fabio Quartararo at the final corner at Buriram on 6 October, having taken pole days after fracturing a bone in his shoulder in a practice crash. Four rounds still remained. The season ended as the most statistically dominant the class has seen: 420 points, twelve wins from nineteen starts and eighteen podiums, all single-season records, with Andrea Dovizioso finishing 151 points behind.

2018.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Motegi, 21 October 2018, three rounds to spare
2018.note: Motegi again, and again at Dovizioso's expense. Márquez took the lead with three laps left on 21 October 2018, and his rival, who needed to outscore him by two points to keep the fight alive, lost the front into the Turn 10 hairpin on the penultimate lap. The win sealed a fifth premier-class title with three rounds remaining and made Márquez, at twenty-five, the youngest rider to reach five, a year younger than Rossi managed in 2005.

2017.clinched: Valencian Community Grand Prix, Valencia, 12 November 2017, final round
2017.note: The 2017 title needed the Valencia finale and nearly slipped away inside it. Márquez led early, then ran wide and saved a near-certain crash with Dovizioso directly behind him; the Ducati rider crashed out of contention moments later. Third place was enough for a fourth premier-class crown at twenty-four. The thirty-seven-point final margin flattered a season in which Márquez fell twenty-seven times and still won it.

2016.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Motegi, 16 October 2016, three rounds to spare
2016.note: Márquez won at Motegi on 16 October 2016 while both Yamahas threw the season away in front of him: Rossi crashed out of the lead battle on lap seven, and Lorenzo, needing a podium to stay alive, lost the front with five laps left. The title was settled with three rounds still to run. Márquez had spent that year riding for points rather than victories, taking five wins in a season of nine different winners.

2015.clinched: Valencian Community Grand Prix, Valencia, 8 November 2015, final round
2015.note: The 2015 championship was decided in the ugliest circumstances of the modern era. Rossi started the Valencia finale from the back of the grid, the penalty for the Sepang clash with Márquez, and rode through to fourth. Lorenzo simply won from pole, his seventh victory of the year, and took the title by five points. Rossi needed both Hondas to finish behind Lorenzo, and Márquez crossed the line 0.263 seconds adrift of him.

2014.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Motegi, 12 October 2014, three rounds to spare
2014.note: Márquez opened 2014 with ten straight wins and still could not settle the title until round fifteen, crashes at Misano and Aragón having delayed the arithmetic. Second place behind Lorenzo at Motegi on 12 October did it, three rounds early, and at twenty-one he became the youngest back-to-back premier-class champion. The thirteen victories he finished with remain the single-season record, and he had missed most of pre-season testing with a leg broken in training.

2013.clinched: Valencian Community Grand Prix, Valencia, 10 November 2013, final round
2013.note: A rookie won the 2013 championship, which had not happened since Kenny Roberts in 1978. Márquez needed fourth place at the Valencia finale and took third from his ninth pole of the season, leaving Lorenzo and Pedrosa to fight it out ahead of him. At twenty years and 266 days he replaced Freddie Spencer as the youngest premier-class champion, a record that had stood since 1983, and the final margin over Lorenzo was four points.

2012.clinched: Australian Grand Prix, Phillip Island, 28 October 2012, one round to spare
2012.note: Lorenzo's second title arrived at Phillip Island on 28 October 2012 with a round still to run, and it arrived the awkward way: Dani Pedrosa, twenty-three points behind and needing everything, slid out at the Honda hairpin on lap two, his first mistake of the season. Lorenzo, running second behind a dominant Casey Stoner, chose the championship over the race and settled for the points that made him Spain's first double premier-class champion.

2011.clinched: Australian Grand Prix, Phillip Island, 16 October 2011, two rounds to spare
2011.note: Stoner clinched his second premier-class title at Phillip Island on 16 October 2011, his twenty-sixth birthday, at the circuit he had made his own. He led every lap for a fifth consecutive win there, matching Rossi's record at the track, and needed only sixth place after Lorenzo withdrew following a warm-up crash that cost him part of a finger. It was Honda's first premier-class championship since 2006, and Stoner became the fifth rider to win titles with two manufacturers.

2010.clinched: Malaysian Grand Prix, Sepang, 10 October 2010, three rounds to spare (round 15 of 18)
2010.note: Lorenzo took his first premier-class title at Sepang on 10 October 2010, where third place behind race winner Valentino Rossi was enough with three rounds still to run. Dani Pedrosa, the only rider who could still have caught him, had fractured his collarbone at Motegi and did not start. Lorenzo finished the year on 383 points to Pedrosa's 245, a premier-class record at the time and ten more than Rossi had scored in 2008, built on nine wins and a podium in thirteen of the first fifteen races. He was the second Spaniard to win the premier class, after Àlex Crivillé in 1999.

2009.clinched: Malaysian Grand Prix, Sepang, 25 October 2009, one round to spare (round 16 of 17)
2009.note: Rossi settled his second title in a row at a wet Sepang on 25 October 2009, taking third behind race winner Casey Stoner while Jorge Lorenzo, his Yamaha teammate and the only rider still in contention, could manage only fourth. It was Rossi's seventh premier-class crown, his ninth world championship across all classes, and the fourth he had won for Yamaha. He ended the season on 306 points to Lorenzo's 261, the pair having won between them everything the other two Yamaha and Honda riders left, while Stoner's own defence collapsed under a mystery illness that cost him three races.

2008.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Motegi, 28 September 2008, three rounds to spare (round 15 of 18)
2008.note: Rossi won at Motegi on 28 September 2008 to take the championship back after two seasons without it, passing Casey Stoner under braking on lap 14 and pulling clear to finish 1.943 seconds ahead of him. It was his fifth win in a row and his eighth of the year, and it left Stoner mathematically beaten with three rounds still to run. The title was Rossi's sixth in the premier class and his eighth overall, and the first he had won on Bridgestone tyres. He closed the season on 373 points to Stoner's 280.

2007.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Motegi, 23 September 2007, three rounds to spare (round 15 of 18)
2007.note: Stoner needed only to finish the wet-dry race at Motegi on 23 September 2007, and sixth place behind winner Loris Capirossi did it while Rossi came home thirteenth. It was the first year of the 800cc rules and Stoner had won ten of the eighteen races on the Ducati, ending the season on 367 points to Dani Pedrosa's 242. The championship was Ducati's first in the premier class and the first for a non-Japanese manufacturer since MV Agusta in 1974, as well as Bridgestone's first. Stoner was 21, the youngest premier-class champion since Freddie Spencer in 1983.

2006.clinched: Valencian Community Grand Prix, Valencia, 29 October 2006, final round (17 of 17)
2006.note: Hayden arrived at Valencia on 29 October 2006 eight points behind Rossi and left it champion. Rossi crashed on the fifth lap and recovered only to thirteenth, while Hayden's third place behind Troy Bayliss and Loris Capirossi was worth the five points that decided it, 252 to 247. Hayden won only two races that year against Rossi's five, but he retired just once in a season the Italian spent crashing and breaking down. He was the first American premier-class champion since Kenny Roberts Jr. in 2000, and remains the last.

2005.clinched: Malaysian Grand Prix, Sepang, 25 September 2005, four rounds to spare (round 13 of 17)
2005.note: Rossi's fifth premier-class title in a row was settled at Sepang on 25 September 2005, where second place behind Loris Capirossi was enough with four rounds still to run. He finished the season on 367 points to Marco Melandri's 220, a margin of 147, with eleven wins from seventeen starts, and Yamaha took the manufacturers' and teams' championships alongside it. It was his seventh world championship in all and his second for Yamaha. It was also the end of the run: three seasons would pass before he won another.

2004.clinched: Australian Grand Prix, Phillip Island, 17 October 2004, one round to spare (round 15 of 16)
2004.note: Rossi beat Sete Gibernau by 0.097 seconds after a last-lap fight at Phillip Island on 17 October 2004 and took the title with a round to spare. He had left Honda for Yamaha over the winter, onto a bike that managed a single podium the year before, and won on it at the first attempt: Yamaha's first premier-class championship since Wayne Rainey in 1992. He ended the year on 304 points to Gibernau's 257 with nine wins, a fourth premier-class crown and a third in a row.

2003.clinched: Malaysian Grand Prix, Sepang, 12 October 2003, two rounds to spare (round 14 of 16)
2003.note: Rossi won from pole at Sepang on 12 October 2003, his seventh victory of the year, to settle the championship with two rounds left and only fifty points still on the table. Sete Gibernau, second in the race, was the last rider who could have caught him. Rossi closed the season on 357 points to Gibernau's 277 with nine wins, a third consecutive premier-class title and a fifth world championship across the classes. It was his last season with Honda: he moved to Yamaha for 2004 and won there too.

2002.clinched: Rio Grand Prix, Rio de Janeiro, 21 September 2002, four rounds to spare (round 12 of 16)
2002.note: Rossi won a wet, chaotic race at Rio de Janeiro to take the first championship of the MotoGP era, the season in which 990cc four-strokes replaced the 500cc two-strokes in the premier class. His nearest rival Tohru Ukawa crashed out in the opening laps, and Rossi, having run behind Kenny Roberts Jr. for the first half of the twenty-four, led to the flag ahead of Max Biaggi with four rounds and 100 points still to come. He finished the year on 355 points to Biaggi's 215, with eleven wins from sixteen races on Honda's RC211V. Accounts differ on the day: some archives date the race to Sunday 22 September, while the contemporary race reports place it on Saturday 21 September, which is the date used here.

2001.clinched: Australian Grand Prix, Phillip Island, 14 October 2001, two rounds to spare (round 14 of 16)
2001.note: Rossi took the lead on the last lap at Phillip Island on 14 October 2001 and won by 0.013 seconds from Max Biaggi, clinching the final 500cc World Championship with two rounds to spare. Nine riders crossed the line inside 2.832 seconds of each other. At 22 he became the first rider since Phil Read in 1973 to hold titles in the 125cc, 250cc and 500cc classes, and the first Italian 500cc champion since Franco Uncini in 1982. He finished on 325 points to Biaggi's 219 with eleven wins, and kept his number 46 rather than take the champion's number one.

2000.clinched: Rio de Janeiro Grand Prix, 7 October 2000, two rounds to spare (round 14 of 16)
2000.note: Kenny Roberts Jr. finished sixth at Rio on 7 October 2000, which was enough to settle the title with two rounds to spare, in a race won by the rookie Valentino Rossi. He had taken the championship lead at the third round in Japan and never gave it back, winning four races, one more than anyone else, with nine podiums and a single retirement all year. He and his father Kenny Roberts are the only father and son to have won premier-class titles, twenty years apart. It was also Suzuki's last world championship until Joan Mir's in 2020. He finished on 258 points to Rossi's 209.

1999.clinched: Rio de Janeiro Grand Prix, 24 October 1999, one round to spare (round 15 of 16)
1999.note: Crivillé came through from eleventh on the grid to sixth at Rio on 24 October 1999, and left Brazil 45 points clear with one round to go: the first Spanish rider to win the premier class. The season had turned at the third round in Jerez, where Mick Doohan crashed in wet qualifying and took the injuries that ended his career. Crivillé, his Repsol Honda team-mate, won that race from pole with the fastest lap, and won six in all. He finished the year on 267 points to Kenny Roberts Jr.'s 220.

1998.clinched: Australian Grand Prix, Phillip Island, 4 October 1998, one round to spare (round 13 of 14)
1998.note: Doohan won at Phillip Island on 4 October 1998, from pole and in front of his own crowd, and took a fifth consecutive title with one round left and a 38-point lead Max Biaggi could not close. The season had opened with a shock, the 500cc rookie Biaggi winning at Suzuka, and Àlex Crivillé led the standings at mid-season while Doohan took two retirements. Doohan answered with four straight wins to close the year, eight in all, and Honda won every race but one, Simon Crafar's at Donington. He ended on 260 points to Biaggi's 208.

1997.clinched: British Grand Prix, Donington Park, 17 August 1997, four rounds to spare (round 11 of 15)
1997.note: Doohan took pole, the fastest lap and the win at Donington on 17 August 1997, and with it a fourth straight title, four rounds early. It was the most dominant premier-class season anyone has had: twelve wins from fifteen races, ten of them in a row, and 340 points to 197 for Tadayuki Okada. Twelve wins in a season broke Giacomo Agostini's record, and Honda won every round, the last time a single manufacturer has swept a premier-class year.

1996.season: fifteen rounds in 1996, and the most one-sided of five consecutive titles
1996.note: Doohan won eight of the fifteen rounds, four of them in succession at Jerez, Mugello, Paul Ricard and Assen, and finished 309 points to 245 over his Repsol Honda teammate Àlex Crivillé. Honda filled the top three places in the standings, Luca Cadalora taking third. Daryl Beattie, the rider who had pushed Doohan hardest the year before, took head injuries in a pre-season crash and crashed again in Spain and France, which effectively ended his career.

1995.clinched: Argentine Grand Prix, Buenos Aires, 24 September 1995, one round to spare (round 12 of 13)
1995.note: Doohan won at Buenos Aires on 24 September 1995 with Daryl Beattie second behind him, and took a second title with a round to spare. Beattie had led the championship early, winning at Suzuka and the Nürburgring while Doohan crashed out in Spain and Germany, and it was a practice crash at Assen that ended the Suzuki rider's challenge. Doohan won seven races and finished on 248 points to Beattie's 215, which is the closest anyone came to him across his five title years.

1994.clinched: Czech Republic Grand Prix, Brno, 21 August 1994, three rounds to spare (round 11 of 14)
1994.note: Doohan won at Brno on 21 August 1994 and could no longer be caught with three races still to run, taking the first of his five consecutive titles. He won nine of the fourteen rounds and finished every race on the rostrum, closing the year on 317 points to Luca Cadalora's 174. It was his first championship since the Assen crash of 1992 that nearly cost him his right leg, and the point at which the 500cc class became his.

1993.clinched: United States Grand Prix, Laguna Seca, 12 September 1993, one round to spare (round 13 of 14)
1993.note: Schwantz's only world championship was settled by the worst kind of luck. He arrived at Misano on 5 September 1993 eleven points behind Wayne Rainey; Rainey led the race, lost the rear of the Yamaha and was left paralysed, his career over. Schwantz took the title a week later at Laguna Seca, finishing fourth. Both men won four races that year, and Schwantz had been on the podium in the first nine rounds before a wrist injury at Donington, in contact with Mick Doohan, cost him the points lead. He finished on 248 points to Rainey's 214.

1992.clinched: South African Grand Prix, 6 September 1992, final round (13 of 13)
1992.note: Rainey needed a two-point swing in the last race of 1992 and got it, finishing third while Doohan, back on the bike, came home sixth. Doohan had won the first four rounds, the first rider to open a season that way since Giacomo Agostini in 1972, and was running away with the championship when he crashed at Assen and broke both bones in his lower right leg. A botched operation nearly cost him the leg and he missed four races; Rainey scored in every one of them and took a third consecutive title, 140 to 136.

1991.clinched: Vitesse du Mans Grand Prix, Bugatti Circuit, 8 September 1991, one round to spare (round 14 of 15)
1991.note: With ten laps left at Le Mans on 8 September 1991, Rainey needed only to hold third place, and he held it, behind Kevin Schwantz and Mick Doohan, for a second consecutive title with a round to spare. Doohan pushed him all year and led the standings after the Spanish round; Rainey answered with six wins, among them a last-lap fight at Brno and a defence of the Mistral straight at Paul Ricard where he zigzagged to stop Doohan getting a run at him. He finished on 233 points to Doohan's 224.

1990.clinched: Czechoslovak Grand Prix, Brno, 26 August 1990, two rounds to spare (round 13 of 15)
1990.note: Rainey needed a third place in one of the last three races and won at Brno instead, in front of a crowd of about 100,000, ahead of Wayne Gardner and Eddie Lawson. Kevin Schwantz had taken pole and crashed out of third with his bike on fire. Rainey won seven races that year and finished on the podium in fourteen of the fifteen rounds, closing on 255 points to Schwantz's 188, having switched from Dunlop tyres to Michelin over the winter. It was the first of his three consecutive titles.

1989.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Goiânia, 17 September 1989, final round (15 of 15)
1989.note: Lawson finished second behind Kevin Schwantz at Goiânia on 17 September 1989, with Wayne Rainey third, and took a fourth title on the last day of the season. He had left Yamaha over the winter for a Honda satellite team, a move most people expected to fail, and so became the first rider to win consecutive premier-class championships on two different makes of machine. The final margin was 228 to 210.5, and the half point is real: the FIM halved the scores for the rain-drenched Belgian Grand Prix after the organisers restarted it three times against the regulations.

1988.clinched: No race clinched it: Brno was run on 28 August 1988, and the cancellation of the Argentine Grand Prix then left one round in which Wayne Gardner could not close a twenty-point gap
1988.note: The 1988 championship was settled by a cancellation. Lawson led Gardner by twenty points after Brno with two races left on the original calendar, and the Argentine Grand Prix was then dropped for bad organisation and unsafe track conditions. With only Goiânia to come, Gardner could at best have drawn level on points, and Yamaha's account of the season says the count-back on wins would still have gone to Lawson. Lawson won at Goiânia anyway, ahead of Gardner and Kevin Schwantz, and finished on 252 points to Gardner's 229 for a third title.

1987.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Goiânia, 27 September 1987, one round to spare (round 14 of 15)
1987.note: Gardner took pole, the fastest lap and the win at Goiânia on 27 September 1987, and with a round still to run became Australia's first premier-class world champion. He won seven of the fifteen races and scored in every one of them, finishing on 178 points to Randy Mamola's 158, with Eddie Lawson third a single point behind Mamola despite five wins of his own. His race engineer that year was Jeremy Burgess, who went on to run Mick Doohan's five titles and Valentino Rossi's seven.

1986.season: eleven rounds in 1986, with the champion winning the finale at Misano
1986.note: Lawson took a second premier-class title in three years by winning seven of the eleven rounds, four of them consecutively at Monza, the Nürburgring, the Salzburgring and Rijeka, and closed the year by winning at Misano on 24 August. He finished 139 points to 117 over Wayne Gardner. The season belonged as much to who was absent: Freddie Spencer, who had taken both the 250cc and 500cc championships in 1985, developed carpal tunnel syndrome, started only two rounds, and never won another grand prix.

1985.clinched: Swedish Grand Prix, Anderstorp, 11 August 1985, one round to spare (round 11 of 12)
1985.note: Spencer won from pole at Anderstorp on 11 August 1985 ahead of Eddie Lawson, and completed the only 250cc and 500cc double anyone has managed in one season: the 250 title had been settled a week earlier at a wet Silverstone, where he won the 500 race as well. He took seven premier-class wins from twelve rounds and finished on 141 points to Lawson's 133. Anderstorp was also the last grand prix win of his career. He was 23.

1984.clinched: Swedish Grand Prix, Anderstorp, 12 August 1984, one round to spare (round 11 of 12)
1984.note: Lawson took the lead on the last lap at Anderstorp on 12 August 1984 to win the race and the championship, while Randy Mamola, the only rider who could still have caught him, crashed out unhurt. It was Lawson's first title and it came in his second season of grand prix racing, having led the standings from the first round to the last and crashed only twice all year, both times in practice. Sweden was his final win of the season; he finished on 142 points to Mamola's 111.

1983.clinched: San Marino Grand Prix, Imola, 4 September 1983, final round (12 of 12)
1983.note: Spencer arrived at Imola on 4 September 1983 five points clear of Kenny Roberts, who had to win the race with Spencer third or lower. Roberts won it; Spencer finished second, 1.230 seconds behind, with Eddie Lawson third, and the championship went to Spencer by two points, 144 to 142. The two had matched each other all season, six wins and three second places each and six poles each, and it had turned a month earlier at Anderstorp, where Spencer dived inside Roberts at the second-to-last corner, sent them both wide, and recovered first to win by under two tenths. It was 23 years before another title fight reached the final race.

1982.season: fourteen rounds in 1982, a season remembered for its casualties
1982.note: Uncini won the championship for Suzuki with 103 points to 76 over Graeme Crosby, and almost everything else about the year was damage. Most of the factory riders boycotted the French round at Nogaro over unsafe track conditions. Barry Sheene hit the obscured fallen machine of Patrick Igoa in practice at Silverstone and broke both legs and an arm. Kenny Roberts hurt a finger and a knee at the same British Grand Prix and missed the rest of the season. Freddie Spencer, in his first full year, finished third.

1981.season: fourteen rounds in 1981, won from an independent team
1981.note: Lucchinelli beat the factory-supported effort with a privateer entry, riding for the Italian Nava Gallina squad while his closest rival Randy Mamola had the Heron Suzuki machinery run by the British importer. Lucchinelli found the decisive run in midsummer, four victories in five races at Assen, Spa, Imola and Imatra, and finished 105 points to 94. Kenny Roberts, three times champion, was a distant third.

1980.season: eight rounds in 1980, two of them cancelled outright
1980.note: Roberts won the first three races of the year at Misano, Jarama and Paul Ricard, won nothing after that, and still took a third consecutive title 87 points to 72 over Randy Mamola. The calendar lost the Venezuelan round and an Austrian Grand Prix abandoned in snow, the last grand prix to have all of its races cancelled until the British round of 2018. Roberts won the riders' championship on a Yamaha in a year Suzuki won the constructors'.

1979.season: thirteen rounds in 1979, the year the riders took on the governing body
1979.note: Roberts won five races and finished 113 points to 89 over Virginio Ferrari, but the season mattered for something other than the result. The leading riders boycotted the Belgian Grand Prix at Spa over the state of a newly laid surface, then threatened to leave and set up a rival World Series championship altogether. The threat worked, prize money and professional standards improved, and the man who led it won the title as well.

1978.clinched: German Grand Prix, Nürburgring, 20 August 1978, final round
1978.note: Roberts arrived at the Nürburgring eight points clear of the defending champion Barry Sheene and needed only to stay near the front. He finished third behind Virginio Ferrari and Johnny Cecotto and became the first American to win a world championship in grand prix road racing, in his first full season in Europe. He took it 110 points to 100, with four wins to Sheene's two, and did it on one Yamaha while the factory's lead rider had two better bikes.

1977.season: thirteen rounds in 1977, and a second consecutive title
1977.note: Sheene won six of the thirteen rounds, opening at San Carlos in Venezuela and adding Hockenheim, Imola, Paul Ricard, Spa and Anderstorp, to finish 107 points to 80 over Steve Baker. The Austrian Grand Prix was reduced to a shell: after a catastrophic accident in the 350cc race the 500cc riders went on strike, the organisers ran the race anyway with a depleted field, and Jack Findlay won it.

1976.season: twelve rounds in 1976, and a first title for its champion
1976.note: Sheene's first championship came with five wins and a margin of 72 points to 48 over Teuvo Länsivuori, Suzuki riders filling all three top places. The season closed two eras at once. The Isle of Man TT, boycotted for years by the leading riders over safety, ran for the last time as a championship round. And at the Nürburgring, Giacomo Agostini took the last grand prix victory of his career, which was also the last premier-class win for a four-stroke engine.

1975.clinched: Czechoslovak Grand Prix, Brno, the tenth and final round of 1975
1975.note: Agostini needed only a top-seven finish at Brno and took it, declining to race Phil Read for the win. It was the first premier-class title for a two-stroke machine, the first for Yamaha in the class, and the first for a manufacturer from outside Europe. It was also the fifteenth and last world championship of his career. Read scored more points across the season than Agostini did, but only a rider’s best six results counted, and on that basis Agostini won it 84 points to 76.

1974.season: twelve rounds in 1974, and the last world championship MV Agusta ever won
1974.note: Read took a second premier-class title with four wins, finishing 82 points to 69 over his MV Agusta teammate Gianfranco Bonera. Agostini had left for Yamaha and, troubled by injuries, won the 350cc championship instead, the fourteenth world title of his career. MV Agusta's crown was its seventeenth consecutive one in the class and the last it would win in any, and in the same season the marque lost the constructors' championship to Yamaha.

1973.season: twelve rounds in 1973, decided inside the MV Agusta team
1973.note: Read was signed as Agostini’s teammate and declined to behave like one, scoring at every opportunity while Agostini took no points at all from the first seven races. Read finished 84 points to 63 over Kim Newcombe, a New Zealander racing a machine built around a Dieter König outboard engine, with Agostini third. The defining event of the year was the Nations Grand Prix at Monza, cancelled after a first-lap chain accident in the 250cc race that involved more than a dozen riders and killed Renzo Pasolini and Jarno Saarinen.

1972.season: thirteen rounds in 1972, eleven of them won by the champion
1972.note: Agostini's eleven victories in a thirteen-round season gave him a sixth consecutive premier-class title, 105 points to 87 over his MV Agusta teammate Alberto Pagani, out of 165 he actually scored before the counting rules were applied. The year also had a lasting consequence. Gilberto Parlotti was killed at the Isle of Man TT, and Agostini, who had won the 500cc race there, never rode the event again and campaigned against it. It lost championship status after 1976.

1971.season: eleven rounds in 1971, with the champion sitting out the last of them
1971.note: Agostini had the championship won before the closing Spanish Grand Prix and did not start it. He finished 90 points to 58 over Keith Turner, a New Zealand privateer on a Coleman Suzuki, and the third-placed rider was on a Suzuki as well. Almost no factory opposition was left in the class: MV Agusta's rivals were privateers on ageing machinery, and the real threat was forming in the 350cc class, where Jarno Saarinen's Yamaha was closing.

1970.season: twelve rounds in 1970, in the middle of the most one-sided run the class has seen
1970.note: Between 1968 and 1970 Agostini won every race he started in both the 350cc and 500cc classes, and this season sat in the middle of it. He finished 90 points to 62 over Ginger Molloy, the second of three New Zealanders to take the premier-class runner-up place in four seasons. Angelo Bergamonti was third, and won the closing Spanish round.

1969.season: twelve rounds in 1969, and the maximum score the rules permitted
1969.note: Only a rider’s best seven results counted, and Agostini banked all seven as wins for 105 points, out of 150 he actually scored across the season. The runner-up, Gyula Marsovszky, managed 47 on a privateer Linto. With Honda gone there was no factory rival left, MV Agusta was racing privateers on old machinery, and a fourth consecutive premier-class title was never in doubt.

1968.season: ten rounds in 1968, and ten wins
1968.note: Agostini won every round of the season, the only perfect premier-class campaign of his career, and finished 48 points to 34 over the Australian privateer Jack Findlay. The field had thinned for a specific reason: the FIM's new regulations favoured two-strokes, Honda's policy was to race four-strokes only, and the company withdrew from motorcycle racing to concentrate on Formula One. Mike Hailwood left bikes for cars in the same move.

1967.clinched: Grand Prix of Canada, Mosport, 30 September 1967, final round
1967.note: Agostini needed a single point at Mosport and rode for exactly that. Hailwood tried to draw him into a fight, letting him lead and then repassing him at will on the back straight, and when the Italian would not take the bait he cleared off to win by 38 seconds. Agostini finished second, and the two ended level on 46 points to 46, each with five wins. The championship went to Agostini on second places, three against Hailwood's two. Neither had finished lower than second all year.

1966.season: eight rounds in 1966, and a first premier-class title
1966.note: Agostini's first 500cc championship was won against a faster motorcycle. Only the best five results counted, and he finished 36 points to 30 over Mike Hailwood, whose Honda took three of the last six races without closing the gap. Honda swept all five constructors' championships that season, the 500cc one included, so Agostini and MV Agusta took the riders' title in a class the opposition's manufacturer won.

1965.season: a fourth consecutive premier-class title in 1965
1965.note: Hailwood won it comfortably, finishing 48 points to 38 over his own MV Agusta teammate Giacomo Agostini, in the last season before Agostini took the class off him. Only the best six results counted. Hailwood won both the opening race at Daytona and the last at Suzuka, on a calendar that had grown to thirteen grands prix.

1964.season: a third consecutive premier-class title in 1964
1964.note: Hailwood won seven races and finished 40 points to 25 over Jack Ahearn, an Australian on a privateer Norton, with only his best five results counting out of the 56 he actually scored. That a privateer Norton finished second says most of what needs saying about the state of the 500cc class: MV Agusta had the only competitive factory machine in it.

1963.season: eight rounds in 1963, seven of them won by the champion
1963.note: Hailwood won everything except the Dutch TT, which went to John Hartle, and closed the season with five straight victories in the Ulster, East German, Finnish, Nations and Argentine rounds. He finished 40 points to 21 over Alan Shepherd on a Matchless, with Hartle third on a Gilera. Only his best five results counted, out of 56 scored.

1962.season: a first premier-class title in 1962, inherited in the worst way
1962.note: Hailwood was MV Agusta's second rider behind the reigning double champion Gary Hocking. On the second lap of the Junior TT on 6 June, Hocking's close friend Tom Phillis crashed fatally at Laurel Bank. Hocking won the Senior TT that same week, flew to Italy to tell Count Agusta he was finished, and retired from motorcycle racing. Hailwood won five of the remaining rounds and took the championship 40 points to 29 over Alan Shepherd, the first of his four.

1961.season: a double championship in 1961, and a career over within a year
1961.note: Hocking became MV Agusta’s lead rider when John Surtees left for Formula One, and won both the 350cc and 500cc titles, taking seven of the nine 500cc grands prix he started and twelve races across the two classes. He finished 48 points to 40 over his teammate Mike Hailwood. He would win the Senior TT the following June, retire days later after Tom Phillis was killed at the same meeting, switch to cars, and be killed that December in practice for the Natal Grand Prix at Durban in a Lotus-Climax.

1960.season: a fourth and final premier-class title in 1960
1960.note: Surtees took his last 500cc championship 32 points to 26 over his MV Agusta teammate Remo Venturi, with only the best four results counting, which was also the most the rules allowed anyone to score. He then left motorcycles for Formula One and became the only person to win world championships on two wheels and on four.

1959.season: a third consecutive premier-class title in 1959
1959.note: Surtees won every 500cc race he started and retained both the 350cc and 500cc championships, finishing 32 points to 22 over Remo Venturi out of 56 he actually scored. MV Agusta took the top two places in the standings, and the Nortons behind them could not get close.

1958.season: a second premier-class title in 1958, at the start of a monopoly
1958.note: At the end of the previous season Gilera, Mondial, Moto Guzzi and MV Agusta had all announced they were leaving grand prix racing, blaming rising costs and falling motorcycle sales. MV Agusta changed its mind, and the consequence was seventeen consecutive 500cc championships. Surtees won six of the seven rounds of the first of them, losing only the Swedish Grand Prix to Geoff Duke, and finished 32 points to 20 over his teammate John Hartle. Duke, by then a four-time champion, was third.

1957.season: a first and only premier-class title in 1957, and Gilera’s last
1957.note: Liberati won four of the six rounds for Gilera and finished 32 points to 20 over his own teammate Bob McIntyre, who had won the Senior TT that year. It was the last 500cc championship Gilera would take. Before the season was over the Italian factories announced they would leave grand prix racing at the end of it, citing escalating costs and dwindling motorcycle sales, and of the four only MV Agusta came back.

1956.season: a first premier-class title in 1956, and MV Agusta’s first
1956.note: Surtees won the first three rounds, at the Isle of Man, Assen and Spa, and that was enough: 24 points to 16 over Walter Zeller on a BMW. The defending champion missed half the season. Geoff Duke was serving a six-month ban for supporting a strike by privateer riders over starting money at the 1955 Dutch TT, and returned in time to win the Nations Grand Prix at Monza.

1955.season: a third consecutive title in 1955, and the last of four
1955.note: Duke's final championship was the closest of his three with Gilera: 36 points to 30 over his teammate Reg Armstrong, with Umberto Masetti, himself twice a champion, third on an MV Agusta. Duke won the Dutch TT that year and also backed the privateers who struck there over starting money, and the FIM banned him for the first six months of the following season.

1954.season: a second consecutive title in 1954, at double the runner-up’s score
1954.note: Duke won five grands prix in a row for Gilera, taking the Belgian, Dutch, German, Swiss and Nations rounds, and finished 40 points to 20 over Ray Amm of Southern Rhodesia on a Norton, exactly twice his total. Ken Kavanagh was third on a Moto Guzzi. The Ulster 500cc race was stopped by bad weather and the FIM struck it from the championship.

1953.season: a first title with Gilera in 1953, after leaving Norton
1953.note: Duke left the Norton team that had made him a champion and won at the first attempt with Gilera, taking four grands prix and finishing 38 points to 24 over Reg Armstrong, with Alfredo Milani third and Gilera machines in all three places. At the German Grand Prix every factory team withdrew from the 350cc and 500cc races, having pronounced the circuit unsafe before practice had begun.

1952.season: a second and final title in 1952, by three points
1952.note: Masetti took it 28 points to 25 over Leslie Graham, the first world champion of all, who by then had moved to MV Agusta. Only the best five results counted. Graham won the last two rounds of the year, the Nations and Spanish grands prix, and still lost it, because Masetti had banked enough before them. Reg Armstrong was third on a Norton.

1951.season: a first premier-class title in 1951, and the last for a British machine
1951.note: Duke won the 350cc and 500cc championships in the same season for Norton, finishing 35 points to 31 over Alfredo Milani on a Gilera. No constructor from outside Japan or Italy has won the premier class in the years since. Umberto Masetti, the defending champion, was third.

1950.season: a first title in 1950, by a single point
1950.note: Masetti won the second world championship 28 points to 27 over Geoff Duke, across six rounds in which only a rider's best four results counted. Masetti won at Spa and Assen, Duke won the Ulster and Nations rounds, and the dropped-score rule took a point off Masetti that he had already earned. Duke lost the riders' title, but Norton won the constructors' championship.

1949.season: the first world championship season, in 1949
1949.note: The championship began on 17 June 1949 and ran for six rounds. Graham won the Swiss and Ulster grands prix on the AJS Porcupine and finished on 30 points, one clear of Nello Pagani’s Gilera, and he did it while being comprehensively outscored: Pagani took 40 points across the season against Graham’s 31 before the counting rules were applied, only a rider’s best results being admitted. Arciso Artesiani was third.
